In summary
Proposition 40 would levy a one-time tax on billionaires. Some say the initiative opens the door to tax flight and more aggressive taxation. Others say there’s no way to predict the outcome.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), also known as the billionaire tax, is the most contentious fight on Californians’ ballots this November.
The proposal to impose a one-time asset tax on the net worth of the state’s approximately 200 billionaires has divided Democrats, galvanized progressives and sparked fierce pushback from business groups and the state’s wealthy tech sector. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has poured $102 million into the campaign against the measure — including two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/) — and is among a handful of billionaires who have moved residences or business assets out of the state in an attempt to avoid the proposed tax. In total, opponents have raised more than $205 million to stop Prop. 40, according to campaign finance records.
It would also set up an entirely new system of taxes in a state that doesn’t traditionally tax wealth. That would be challenging to implement and experts say is sure to invite litigation. Here are some common questions and answers about how the measure would work.
How would the state assess the tax?
Aside from local taxes on real estate and some business equipment, California isn’t in the business of valuing and taxing personal property.
Prop. 40 would require the state, within six months, to create a way to assess the value of a wide range of holdings: billionaires’ stock, investment accounts and business interests, but also their art collections, wine vaults, cars and anything else that stores wealth.
“I have a client who has a machine gun collection,” said Jon Feldhammer, a San Francisco tax attorney who said he is advising several clients who would be or believe they could be subject to the billionaire tax.
The definition of wealth and property has to be broad to close possible loopholes, said Kirk Stark, a UCLA tax law professor.
“Otherwise there would be a very simple workaround, which is, if there’s something that’s exempt then you know there would be an incentive to just shift wealth from one form to another,” Stark said.
Ensuring those subject to the tax aren’t underreporting their assets would require the state’s Franchise Tax Board to hire more people for appraisals and auditing, Stark said.
“It can be done,” he said. “But it’s going to take a huge investment of resources to actually pull it off.”
Franchise Tax Board spokesperson Andrew LePage declined to say how many staff the agency would need to implement Prop. 40. Currently, the board doesn’t appraise property but sometimes auditors “examine asset values reported by taxpayers to ensure accuracy,” he said.
Chris Parker, a former attorney for the tax board who now works as a tax attorney with the firm Baker Tilly, said the board has “no way of knowing anyone’s net wealth.”

Ariel Jurow Kleiman, a tax policy professor at the University of Southern California, doesn’t think the state would have a hard time putting the tax into effect. Stocks, which make up a substantial part of billionaires’ wealth, are easily valued, she said. For more “bespoke” property like art and jewelry, California could look to the Internal Revenue Service’s federal tax on inherited property.
“There are commonsense methods like looking at comparable assets or looking to available markets to see how comps are valued,” she said. “We wouldn’t be asking people to reinvent the wheel here.”
Experts do expect disputes over the value of privately held businesses.

Feldhammer said many startup founders have raised money for their companies but haven’t yet sold any products. He criticized the ballot measure for defining a company’s worth as the most recent amount of investment money it raised, which diverges from how the IRS calculates an asset’s fair market value for the estate tax.
“How do you value a company that is not on the public market? It doesn’t even have a product yet. It’s not making any money,” he said.
He said he expects clients to mount lengthy legal challenges arguing the law overvalues their business holdings.
“These are people who have oftentimes plenty of wealth to spend on legal fees to put up the best defense money can buy,” he said.
Will billionaires leave?
The campaign against the measure warns that billionaires will flee California (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-unions-billionaire-tax-ballot/), depriving the state of billions of dollars in income tax revenue that helps fund the state budget. Experts say there’s no way to know whether the tax will spark a large-scale exodus.
Joel Slemrod, a University of Michigan economics professor who studies tax policy, said there’s very little evidence to gauge how billionaires could react to California’s tax, partly because the proposal is unique.
California experts considering the tax have looked at wealth taxes in European countries to try to discern the impact of Prop. 40. In 1990, 12 countries had wealth taxes. Today, only four remain. Many countries abandoned them because they were difficult and expensive to implement, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/the-role-and-design-of-net-wealth-taxes-in-the-oecd_9789264290303-en.html). But Slemrod said those examples are “not immediately applicable” to Prop. 40 because they differed significantly in design: Tax rates were much lower, they were intended to be permanent and the money was not earmarked for special interests.
“I wouldn’t jump from the evidence we have to California,” Slemrod said.
But one issue that could matter significantly for California, Slemrod said, is that it is much easier to move assets between states than between countries, as sometimes happened in Europe. Spain allowed its provinces to enact wealth taxes and research suggests that rich people changed residences based on tax rates. (https://direct.mit.edu/rest/article-abstract/101/2/214/58521/Relocation-of-the-Rich-Migration-in-Response-to)
Researchers at the Hoover Institution (https://www.hoover.org/research/net-present-value-billionaire-tax-act-assessment-fiscal-effects-californias-proposed), a conservative policy think tank, conducted an analysis suggesting Californians need not look at history to figure out Prop. 40’s impact. Tax flight has already happened. They estimate that billionaires representing 30% of the tax base have publicly said they have left, lowering state revenue estimates by $60 billion and permanently altering California’s income tax collection.
Feldhammer, the tax lawyer, said “a third to half” of his clients have left the state over the proposed tax. He declined to say how many clients that is. Other tax lawyers told CalMatters that clients who are worth less than $1 billion are also considering moving to avoid limiting their earning potential.
Billionaires who didn’t leave before Jan. 1 would face taxes on their assets anyway; the measure would apply to anyone who was a California resident on that date.
But Feldhammer said he expects people to sue over the measure’s retroactive nature, pointing to two U.S. Supreme Court decisions from the 1920s that held it was unconstitutional to apply the federal estate and gift taxes to assets transferred before those laws were enacted. In 1994, the court ruled that retroactive taxes could be constitutional in certain limited circumstances.
Asked how he’s advising clients who are considering leaving California, Feldhammer said there’s a “reasonable argument that the law may be unconstitutionally retroactive — but to take advantage of that, you’re going to have to leave.”
Would it allow the state to tax my retirement?
If you’re not a billionaire, no.
Even for billionaires, Prop. 40 exempts pensions and individual retirement accounts from the asset tax. There are some exceptions, most notably for Roth IRAs that contain more than $10 million.
Misleading advertisements from opponents claim the tax would allow California soon to eat into retirement savings for average Californians. They’re supporting Prop. 42, which would block the proposed billionaire tax by broadly banning any new taxes on personal property such as investment, retirement and pension accounts. Brin’s political spending group, Building a Better California, put it on the ballot, and unions representing firefighters, police and construction workers support it. (If both measures pass, (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/) whichever receives more “yes” votes becomes law.)
Proponents of Prop. 42 say their measure would protect the pensions and retirement accounts of teachers, firefighters and middle-class workers from being taxed before they withdraw the money.
“A new tax on Californians’ retirement and life savings would be devastating,” Robert Gutierrez, president of the California Taxpayers Association, said in a press release.
There are no active proposals to tax those accounts on the ballot or in the Legislature. Lawmakers who have floated such wealth taxes in the past have gotten nowhere.
Still, Brian Marvel, president of the Peace Officers Research Association of California, which supports Prop. 42, denied being deceptive and said it’s “within the realm of realization” for California to tax middle-class workers’ retirement accounts.
“I think it’s more important to be proactive in this area,” he said.
How would the money be used?
Proponents say the billionaire tax is intended to backfill federal cuts to the state’s expansive Medi-Cal health program (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/) for low-income residents. State officials project the cuts, enacted as part of President Donald Trump’s 2025 budget bill known as H.R. 1, could amount to $30 billion a year (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/the-cut-medi-cal-ripple-effects/).
The initiative gives the Legislature broad authority to decide how to spend the money. Of the revenue, 90% percent would be put in a special fund for healthcare; the other 10% would be put in a special fund to pay for schools and food assistance like CalFresh, which was also targeted by federal cuts.
If the money is used to keep Californians on Medi-Cal, that could mean spending it on the private health insurance companies that the state contracts with to administer low-income residents’ coverage.
There is some debate over whether the money would actually offset the cuts to Medi-Cal and how strictly the language bars lawmakers from using the money for anything else.
Opponents such as the California Medical Association and Planned Parenthood recently circulated a memo (https://calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Memo_Health-Care-Funding-Under-Prop-40_9.18.26.pdf) arguing there’s no guarantee the money would replace the federal funding cuts, because the proposition also allows the money to offset state cuts to Medi-Cal. They warn that would allow lawmakers and the governor to use the new tax money to maintain state funding levels for Medi-Cal and free up the state’s general fund to pay for other things.
Lawmakers and governors have in the past used special new funds to simply replace existing funding. Then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, did it with mental health funding created by a voter-approved tax on millionaires, and then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, did it with health funding created by the state tobacco tax. More recently, doctors and hospitals accused Newsom of using a different healthcare tax to backfill the general fund. They placed Proposition 35 on the ballot in 2024 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/11/election-result-proposition-35/) to earmark the money. Voters approved it, but the groups say some funding was still diverted.
But proponents of Prop. 40 said that concern doesn’t make sense: Those budget maneuvers, they said, are usually done to address state budget shortfalls, while Prop. 40 was already written to create funding for a shortfall.
For the record: This story has been updated to correct the amount that Brin has donated to a political action committee opposing Prop. 40 and supporting Props. 41 and 42. He has donated $102 million.

Prop 42 is a measure on the November 3, 2026 ballot (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov_2026_general_pdf_prop42-2Dtext-2Dproposed-2Dlaws.pdf&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=c3Gqu-OMIDatgK3hnMmB3S2ODmqsGQ0poGtXleReCu8&e=) that protects Californians from double taxation on the money we earn by closing a loophole (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__voterguide.sos.ca.gov_propositions_42_&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=ufUF2OJehlbx--9fM7nvGFw4Qh_D0Cgtj_UKws5-HY0&e=) in California’s Constitution that allows new state taxes on retirement accounts, personal savings, pensions, and other personal property.
Updated October 13, 2026
What is Prop 42 (2026)? (javascript:void(0))
Prop 42, the Retirement & Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026, protects Californians from double taxation on the money we earn (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__voterguide.sos.ca.gov_propositions_42_&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=ufUF2OJehlbx--9fM7nvGFw4Qh_D0Cgtj_UKws5-HY0&e=) by closing a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows new state taxes on retirement accounts, personal savings, pensions, and other personal property.
You already pay income taxes when you earn your money. Proposition 42 (2026) ensures the state cannot tax that same money twice simply because it is sitting in a retirement account or savings account. It also prohibits retroactive taxes (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov_2026_general_pdf_prop42-2Dtext-2Dproposed-2Dlaws.pdf&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=c3Gqu-OMIDatgK3hnMmB3S2ODmqsGQ0poGtXleReCu8&e=) that would change the rules after you’ve already earned and saved.
You earned and saved it. Prop 42 (2026) protects it.
Why is Prop 42 Needed? (javascript:void(0))
California is the third most expensive state (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__www.cnbc.com_make-2Dit_2025_01_19_most-2Dexpensive-2Dus-2Dstates-2Dto-2Dretire.html&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=q3QbdWzqFeD9B_wUx9JL86V-tLjHuGtDqGwUv2vctdw&e=) for retirees. Our high cost of living and high taxes already make it difficult for people to get ahead or to save enough for retirement. A recent survey of Californians found that 73% know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
Californians deserve peace of mind that their hard-earned savings will be there when they need them. Yet, California’s Constitution allows the Legislature and special interests to impose new state taxes on retirement accounts and personal savings. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings. Prop 42 (2026) closes that loophole (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov_2026_general_pdf_prop42-2Dtext-2Dproposed-2Dlaws.pdf&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=c3Gqu-OMIDatgK3hnMmB3S2ODmqsGQ0poGtXleReCu8&e=) and protects retirement, life savings and personal property from new taxes.
Can the Legislature Pass Taxes on Retirement & Life Savings Today? (javascript:void(0))
Yes. California's Constitution currently gives the Legislature the authority to impose taxes on personal property such as retirement accounts, pensions, 401(k)s, IRAs, bank accounts, and other personal savings.
In recent years, lawmakers have introduced five separate bills proposing taxes on retirement savings and other personal property. Although none became law, these attempts underscore that this authority already exists and has been tried repeatedly.
The Legislature should not be able to tax retirement accounts. Prop 42 (2026) provides that protection by closing the loophole in California's Constitution before it can be used to tax retirement savings and personal property.
What Does Prop 42 Protect? (javascript:void(0))
Prop 42 (2026) (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__voterguide.sos.ca.gov_propositions_42_&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=ufUF2OJehlbx--9fM7nvGFw4Qh_D0Cgtj_UKws5-HY0&e=) protects retirement accounts, including 401(k)s, pensions, IRAs, and other retirement plans. It also protects personal savings accounts and other personal property that could otherwise be subject to new state taxes.
How Would a Tax on Retirement Savings Affect My 401(k)? (javascript:void(0))
Even a small annual tax on retirement savings could reduce both the value of your retirement savings and the investment growth that helps build retirement security over time.
A recent economic analysis (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__www.morningstar.com_news_pr-2Dnewswire_20260929la57497_10000-2Da-2Dyear-2Dtax-2Don-2Dretirement-2Dnew-2Dreport-2Dshows-2Dhow-2Deven-2Da-2Dsmall-2Dtax-2Don-2Dyour-2Dretirement-2Dcan-2Dhave-2Dhuge-2Dimpact-2Don-2Dyour-2Dfinances&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=ZTMu5TxB_roUrtTd3dWzB9ulnZEAslHk2U4ENj0Fggc&e=) found that even a 1% tax on retirement could cause middle-class Californians to face annual tax bills of up to $10,000 and have to work up to seven additional years before retiring. Prop 42 (2026) protects 401(k)s and other retirement savings from new state taxes that would chip into retirement savings or force Californians to delay retirement.
Does Prop 42 Impact Existing Programs or Funding? (javascript:void(0))
No. Prop 42 (2026) does not reduce existing funding for schools, public safety, healthcare, transportation, or other state programs. It simply prohibits new state taxes on retirement savings and other personal property. Existing revenue sources and funding formulas remain unchanged.
Does Prop 42 Only Protect Wealthy Californians? (javascript:void(0))
No. Prop 42 (2026) protects everyone who works and saves for retirement, including teachers, firefighters, police officers, veterans, retirees, small business owners, and middle-class families. If you have retirement savings or personal savings, Prop 42 (2026) protects you.
Who Supports Prop 42? (javascript:void(0))
Prop 42 (2026) is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, firefighters, veterans, building trades workers, small businesses, and working families who believe Californians should not pay taxes twice on the money they earn and save. This includes the California Professional Firefighters, California Senior Alliance, AMVETS, Dept. of California, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, Peace Officers Research Association of California, and the California Small Business Association.

Endorsement: Yes on Propositions 41 and 42 to limit taxation in California

By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: September 21, 2026 at 2:39 PM PDT | UPDATED: September 21, 2026 at 2:56 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
The most hotly debated initiative on the November ballot is Proposition 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires. As this Editorial Board opined (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/) in our opposition, the union-created Billionaire Tax Act would send a dangerous message to current and future entrepreneurs, and “have a chilling effect on investment.”
But two closely related measures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://www.bakersfield.com/opinion/our-view/our-view-vote-no-on-propositions-40-41-42-tax-propositions-hurt-state-californians/article_1c8492b8-5fb9-4897-9f1c-c9ba56460e0d.amp.html) , have received much less attention — partly because they’re so complicated. By adding related measures to the ballot, opponents of Prop. 40 are hoping that voters approve one of these alternatives that will derail Prop. 40. Because these two measures have elements that contradict Prop. 40, the one that gets the highest vote totals (if voters OK them all) would go into effect.
Adding similar-sounding measures also muddies the waters, thus increasing the likelihood that confused voters vote “no” on all of them — thus accomplishing the main goal of stopping the billionaires’ tax. But our goal isn’t to map out political strategies (https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/nash-game/) . It’s a worthy effort to try to stop a disastrous new tax scheme.
Besides their intended purpose of blocking Prop. 40, the measures could protect taxpayers for years to come.
Specifically, Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. Those audits, which must be completed before the initiative appears on the ballot, would be required to identify ways that such programs could cut annual costs by 10%, per an analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026) from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
While Prop. 40 exempts itself from state spending limits, Prop. 41 also requires new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit (https://www.sheehystrategygroup.com/news/2026/3/9/californias-state-appropriations-limit-gann-limit) — the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year. The state has passed a number of workarounds over the years, but applying new revenues to this formula would potentially require the return of certain additional tax revenues to taxpayers (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41) and the earmarking of revenues to infrastructure.
Prop. 42 is more straightforward. Per theLAO (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=42&year=2026), the initiative prohibits “new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.” California doesn’t currently tax the ownership of financial assets and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees), but the measure’s passage “could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes.” It also limits imposition of retroactive taxes.
So would the Editorial Board support these measures even if they were standalone initiatives? The answers are unequivocal: Yes and yes.

Regarding Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) , California could use better audits of spending programs. It’s a good idea to identify ways to trim existing programs before shoveling more money their way. It is taxpayers’ money, after all. Requiring audits after election officials have collected only 25% of qualifying signatures imposes a relatively costly burden, but those expenses are a rounding error for any major program. We also believe the state should better live up to the terms of the Gann Limit.
Regarding Prop. 42 (https://yesonprop42.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=YesOn42&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24250385746&gbraid=0AAAABEi2smx27CdnofkbhPlt_FqIHXDrD&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHUyIfjJPNFkY5WqUynwZ9APOIPtTZDTa7v5_wEBmvD8nV21v3IkUbhoCCZ8QAvD_BwE) , we endorse its efforts to limit unreasonable future tax increases. G oing back and raising taxes on past earnings (as Prop. 40 does) before the new law was passed is unseemly. Opponents complain that it ties the hands of future Legislatures, but we’re totally fine with putting certain types of assets outside the revenuers’ grasp.
Vote yes on Propositions 41 and 42.

Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Its intentionally punitive and retaliatory cuts to California’s Medicaid program, Medi-Cal, are projected to cost the state billions of dollars per year and lead to more than a million Californians losing access to health care.
In the Bay Area, these cuts are becoming painful.
As our news organization documented this month, the number of uninsured people in emergency rooms at Santa Clara Valley Healthcare and Alameda Health System has spiked year over year.

Those county-run systems expect to collectively lose more than a billion dollars annually. Notably, while our systems and residents are scrambling to survive, rural America is receiving a $50 billion lifeline from House Republicans and President Trump to protect their health care systems.
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.

Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”

That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.

Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo IN SUMMARY Prop. 40 opponents say the billionaire tax allows lawmakers to change the measure with a two-thirds vote. They warn it opens the door to future wealth taxes on everyday Californians. This is only partially true. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. The billionaire tax is a “Trojan horse” for new taxes on all Californians, ads proclaim (https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=1362825008785008&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&sort_data[mode]=total_impressions&sort_data[direction]=desc). But is that true? Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable, the group that paid for the ad, said the message was meant to highlight the policy implications of a wealth tax and the power Prop. 40 gives lawmakers. “Californians deserve to understand those issues and what they could mean for taxpayers and the state’s economy,” Lapsley said in a statement. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Legislative authority Legal experts agree that if Prop. 40 passes, lawmakers would be able to make certain amendments without taking it back to voters. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ The state Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II) allows the Legislature to amend a ballot initiative without another vote if the initiative permits it. That’s a relatively common clause in ballot measures, and Prop. 40 includes it. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). But there isn’t always a clear line for when voters need to approve changes, experts say. “It is common for the Legislature to make amendments,” Colantuono said. “It is (also) common for there to be disputes about those amendments.” ‘Furthers the purposes of’ “Ultimately, it ends up in court,” said Chris Parker, a principal tax attorney at the firm Baker Tilly. The California Supreme Court ruled in a 1995 case (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/11/1243.html) that the Legislature may amend voter-approved laws if the changes can be interpreted as furthering voters’ original goals “by any reasonable construction” — giving lawmakers broad latitude. In 2021, the state Supreme Court held that the Legislature appropriately amended Proposition 57 (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2021/s259011.html), a criminal justice reform measure, by barring the transferring of minors under 16 to adult court. Justices cited the 1995 case, noting that “a strong presumption of constitutionality supports the Legislature’s acts.” Still, the language of the proposition matters. A few years earlier, in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal held that a legislative attempt to allow public funding of political campaigns (https://www4.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the Political Reform Act. Lawmakers responded by passing a new bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) asking voters to weigh in directly — it appears on this year’s ballot as Proposition 4. Judges look at two things, Coluantuono said: what reasonable voters thought they were approving, and whether later legislative changes helped that goal, or got in the way. Certain provisions of Prop. 40 would make it difficult for lawmakers to expand the tax beyond billionaires. The 1995 case established that courts may weigh the language of a ballot measure, arguments printed in the voter guide, and historical context when deciding whether change is consistent with voter intent. Prop. 40’s purpose and intent section (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) says the measure is meant to support healthcare and education “by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth” — referencing billionaire wealth three times. The voter guide arguments similarly target “approximately 200 California billionaires.” “They could probably adjust the structure of the tax in marginal ways, but what they couldn’t do is make it a more than a one-time tax, and they probably couldn’t lower the threshold on wealth,” Coluantuono said. Opponents contend lawmakers could interpret the purpose of the act far more broadly, and a court would agree. They point to the first listed purpose of the initiative that says the tax is meant to “protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs.” Opponents also say the proposal gives the Legislature the authority to change all parts of the initiative, including the constitutional provisions. “Prop 40’s findings and statement of purpose and intent were carefully crafted to ensure that extending the tax to non-billionaires would be consistent with the measure,” said Kurt Oneto, a lawyer for the No on 40 campaign, in a statement. Experts said the question would likely come down to how a court read the act’s purposes. A separate concern: how do you prove wealth? Should Prop. 40 pass, it would create an entirely new tax structure in California — one that assigns a value to very wealthy people’s investments, public and private businesses, as well as personal property such as art or car collections. Valuing something like a tech startup that hasn’t produced a product or gone public could prove especially difficult, Parker said. “The excise tax that’s being proposed here is on potential,” he said. “The question then is, if we open the door to taxing potential, when does that stop?” Lawmakers have periodically tried to pass wealth taxes, but the bills quickly stalled. This marks the first time voters will directly decide on one, making Prop. 40 a crucial test of how much appetite Californians have for his kind of tax structure. Jones said the bigger worry isn’t the tax itself, but other taxes that could follow. “It’s a slippery slope,” she said. Coluantuono said it would still be politically risky for lawmakers to try to implement a wealth tax on everyday Californians, but history shows temporary taxes have more than once become permanent. “When we get a revenue stream in the government and we start spending it on services that people value… there’s tremendous political pressure to prevent the sunset,” he said. Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property's value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
Proposal
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 42 receives more "yes" votes than Proposition 40 on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 42 conflicts with Proposition 40.
Fiscal Effect
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.

However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.
California has changed radically since the 1970s. And its fiscal rules must leave the state with the flexibility to address issues voters of the era never had to deal with — six-figure college costs, seven-figure mortgages and 13-figure wildfire costs.
The state must not surrender its future freedom of action to defeat a single, one-time tax proposal.
Proposition 42
This initiative would prohibit the state from taxing retroactively. And it would permanently ban the state from any new taxes on ownership of financial assets or other personal properties — think stocks, bonds, intellectual property, artwork, etc.
Taxes on wealth are rarely ideal, and our opposition to Proposition 40 reflects that.
However, we are witnessing an explosion of inequality, and the unpredictable course of AI’s development risks supercharging the gap between the haves and have-nots. Joint Venture Silicon Valley’s latest research shows that 78% of Bay Area residents are concerned AI will increase economic inequality.
Proposition 42 was written by this tech boom’s beneficiaries, who are now among the wealthiest humans in history. If this initiative had limited itself to nullifying Proposition 40, we could have supported it. However, amid this era’s technology- and climate-induced uncertainty, California must keep its options open.
Proposition 42 would needlessly and recklessly narrow them.
Reject Propositions 40, 41 and 42.

Not only has Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://calmatters.org/tag/gavin-newsom/) vocally opposed the proposed California billionaire tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/), but he also wants to prevent the state from ever passing a wealth tax in the future. On Friday he endorsed Proposition 42, a ballot measure that would cancel out Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/), the proposed billionaire tax. Prop. 42 would prohibit retroactive taxes like the one-time 5% tax on assets that would apply to any billionaire who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 if Prop. 40 passes. But Prop. 42, funded and placed on the ballot by billionaire and Google co-founder Sergey Brin to defeat the billionaire tax, also would go further, by banning any new taxes on personal property. That includes pensions and 401K accounts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) before retirees start drawing retirement income from them. It also includes other investments, financial assets, business holdings, art collections and all other forms of personal wealth that would be affected by the billionaire tax or any future wealth tax. Newsom’s decision to support Prop. 42 runs counter to his own Democratic Party and some labor unions. It also aligns him with some of the wealthy tech donors with whom he’s maintained longstanding relationships dating back to his days as mayor of San Francisco. Proponents primarily argue that middle-class workers’ retirements and pension accounts should never be taxed as assets before the gains are later taxed a second time as income, even though there is no such proposal (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/). Lawmakers have in the past proposed asset taxes but those bills went nowhere in the Legislature and any tax would require a two-thirds majority to pass. The proposed billionaire tax also exempts many kinds of retirement accounts. “We all agree that Californians deserve to have their retirement and life savings protected from new state taxes so those savings are there when they need them,” Newsom said in a statement released by the proponents, who also include police and fire unions. Proponents of the tax criticized his Prop. 42 endorsement as “in lock step with his billionaire backers.” “By voting yes on Prop 42, he’s showing California his true colors,” said Debru Carthan, vice president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West in a statement. “He’d rather millions of children and families lose their healthcare than ask a couple hundred billionaires to finally pay their fair share.” ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know Newsom has not yet taken a position on Prop. 41, another Brin-backed, anti-billionaire tax measure that would nullify Prop. 40 by subjecting the tax revenues to certain state spending limits and audits, said spokesperson Izzy Gardon. The billionaire tax measure, funded by one healthcare union, would put 90% of the money it collects toward the state’s healthcare program for low-income residents, Medi-Cal (https://calmatters.org/tag/medi-cal/). Newsom, along with many other leading California Democrats and most Republicans, has vocally opposed the billionaire tax and tried to negotiate to keep it off the ballot. In general during his two terms as governor he has opposed state-level taxes on assets, out of concern the wealthy will leave the state and deprive the state of their income tax revenue. The California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) endorsed the billionaire tax and polling shows a slim majority of likely voters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/voters-are-displeased-by-long-ballots-and-split-on-ballot-propositions/) support it. In response to the billionaire tax, Newsom this summer announced a proposal to impose a national tax on the wealthy, including a minimum tax rate on anyone with a net worth of more than $100 million. He also wants to undo corporate tax cuts that President Donald Trump and Congress approved in 2017, boost inheritance taxes and close loopholes the wealthy use to borrow from unrealized capital gains without paying income taxes. Critics from the left have tried to use his Prop. 40 opposition against him. Last weekend as he rallied for the billionaire tax, Democratic California Rep. Ro Khanna, another possible 2028 presidential contender, said donor relations were the “only reason” for Newsom’s opposition. “You can’t be anti-Trump and then do the bidding of Trump donors,” Khanna said in a video (https://www.youtube.com/shorts/ASPHAwXMW5k) with progressive former congressional candidate Saikat Chakrabarti. Khanna pointed to Brin, who has never donated to Newsom but has had a relationship with the governor for years. Newsom and Brin attended each other’s weddings. The tech magnate has recently also turned rightward, courting Trump’s favor. Newsom announced his endorsement of Prop. 42 on Friday along with his positions on most of the 14 ballot measures Californians are deciding on. He endorsed most measures on the ballot, but opposes Proposition 39, the Republican-backed voter ID measure (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-voter-id-proposition-39/); Proposition 43, a measure to make it more difficult (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-prop-43-election-2026/) to pass most local taxes; and Proposition 44, a health union-backed measure (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) to dictate how much money clinics serving low-income patients must spend on patient care. He hasn’t yet taken a position on Proposition 45, the business-backed measure that puts time limits on the environmental review (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/) process for new developments. This paper examines the revenue and migration impact of the 2026 California Billionaire Tax Act, a one-time 5 percent tax on the worldwide net worth of individuals exceeding $1 billion.
Using data from the Forbes Billionaire List, news reports detailing the residential real estate holdings of California billionaires, and public announcements of billionaire departures from the state, we estimate the behavioral response and associated revenue loss to this new tax using several different methodologies.
Even before accounting for reductions in other tax bases such as the income tax, we estimate that the Act will collect approximately $30 billion (range $28 to 36 billion), less than a third of the $100 billion projected by Galle et al. (2025).

Proposition 40 is meant to address the problem of billionaires leaving the state to avoid the tax by making it retroactive and applying it to all taxpayers residing in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026.

The Yes On 40 campaign says NO on 41 & 42
Ballots have been mailed to California voters. The Yes on 40 campaign opposes Propositions 41 and 42.
Initiatives designed to trick voters into undoing Prop 40 How Prop 41 and 42 would hurt California Either measure could undo Prop 40
These initiatives aren’t about helping California. They’re designed to trick voters into undoing Prop 40.
A small group of billionaires including Sergey Brin, John Doerr, Patrick Collison, Eric Schmidt, and Peter Thiel put Prop 41 and 42 on the ballot because they don’t want to pay their fair share. They would rather see ERs and hospitals close and millions of Californians pay more for their healthcare.
Proposition 41 and Prop 42 are not what their proponents say they are. A small group of billionaires who want to avoid paying Prop 40’s one-time tax are spending millions to convince voters these initiatives are about accountability and protecting everyday taxpayers.
Use this guide to learn the truth of what each measure would do, how each could affect Prop 40, and who is funding these campaigns.
How Prop 41 and 42 Would Hurt California
Start with the official text. Then read the Yes on 40 campaign arguments below and see how each could undermine Prop 40 and worsen our state’s healthcare crisis.
Getting ready to vote? Dive into each initiative and understand how each could prevent Prop 40, a one-time, 5% tax on billionaires, from going into full effect.
New audits and spending-limit rules.
Proposition 41 would require new audits for programs funded by certain new special taxes. It would also change how new special tax spending can fit under the state spending limit. [6]
New limits on taxes on personal property.
Prop 42 would ban new state taxes on ownership of financial assets and other personal property. It would also limit some retroactive taxes. [10]
Either measure could undo Prop 40.
This point comes from the state Legislative Analyst.
If Prop 41 or Prop 42 gets more “yes” votes than Prop 40, then Prop 40 could potentially be stopped from becoming law if a court finds the measures conflict. That could happen even if Prop 40 passes but Prop 41 and Prop 42 get more votes, respectively; and courts find that they conflict. That’s why billionaires put Prop 41 and Prop 42 on the ballot: to avoid paying their fair share as their wealth soars. [6] [10]
Why the Yes on 40 campaign is connecting all three measures
Props 41 and 42 are backed by billionaires who oppose Prop 40 and want to keep it from taking effect. The campaign therefore treats all three measures as part of the same ballot fight. Building a Better California is the primary funder of both opposition campaigns, funneling $58.3 million into the Prop 41 campaign and $112.8 million into the Prop 42 campaign. [12]
Prop 40: A one-time wealth tax on billionaires.
The official voter guide says Prop 40 would collect a one-time tax equal to 5% of a billionaire’s wealth. The official title and summary says 90% of the tax revenue goes to healthcare and 10% goes to public education and food assistance programs. [2] [3]
